claims.quote: Once the gustatory cells are activated by the taste molecules, they release neurotransmitters onto the dendrites of sensory neurons. These neurons are part of the facial and glossopharyngeal cranial nerves, as well as a component within the vagus nerve dedicated to the gag reflex.

claims.quote: The Na+ concentration becomes high outside the gustatory cells, creating a strong concentration gradient that drives the diffusion of the ion into the cells. The entry of Na+ into these cells results in the depolarization of the cell membrane and the generation of a receptor potential.

claims.value: Salty and sour tastes are triggered by Na+ and H+ ions, while the other tastes work through G protein–coupled receptors whose signalling depolarizes the cell.
claims.quote: The first two tastes (salty and sour) are triggered by the cations Na+ and H+. The other tastes result from food molecules binding to a G protein–coupled receptor. A G protein signal transduction system ultimately leads to depolarization of the gustatory cell.

claims.value: As a sensory receptor cell, it converts a graded receptor potential in its membrane into neurotransmitter release at its synapses with sensory neurons.
claims.quote: For other sensory receptor cells, such as taste cells or photoreceptors of the retina, graded potentials in their membranes result in the release of neurotransmitters at synapses with sensory neurons. This is called a receptor potential.

tier1.text: Taste receptor cells sense chemicals in the food we eat. These cells sit in clusters called taste buds, inside bumps on the tongue called papillae. Food molecules dissolve in saliva and bind to sensors on microvilli, the hair-like tips of these cells. Once activated, taste receptor cells release chemical signals onto sensory nerve cells.

tier2.text: Taste receptor cells sense chemicals in the food we eat and release neurotransmitters, chemical signals, based on how much of each chemical is present. These cells, also called taste cells, cluster in taste buds, which sit within bumps on the tongue called papillae. Taste cells are long cells whose hair-like tips, called microvilli, reach into a pore in the taste bud. A taste bud's taste cells are replaced every 10 to 14 days. Food molecules dissolve in saliva and then bind to receptors, proteins with a binding site for a specific molecule, on the microvilli. Each of the five primary tastes (sweet, sour, bitter, salty and umami, a savory taste) has its own type of receptor that responds only to that taste. Sour and salty tastes come from ions, atoms with an electric charge, entering the taste cell: hydrogen ions for sour and sodium ions for salty. Sweet, bitter and umami tastes instead need a G protein–coupled receptor, a receptor that activates a G protein to pass the signal on inside the cell. In a taste cell, a change in voltage across the cell membrane leads to the release of neurotransmitters where the cell meets sensory nerve cells. These neurotransmitters can activate sensory nerve cells in the facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves, which are cranial nerves, nerves connected to the brain.
